newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - N.Korea faces bigger food crisis from floods.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - N.Korea faces bigger food crisis from floods.

text.p: Impoverished North Korea is facing more serious food shortages after floods in July wiped out an estimated 373,000 tonnes of cereals, United Nations specialists said on Monday.

They issued their bleak assessment in a special news alert after experts from the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) and the World Food Programme (WFP) visited the country to view damage from floods that hit key farming areas in July.
"It is inevitable that the recent floods will accentuate the seriousness of existing food supply problems in the country," the joint report by the two Rome-based agencies said.

It noted that publicly distributed rations, which cater for most of the population in the secretive communist country, had been cut significantly following severe floods in 1995 and supply difficulties in recent years.
"As a result, rations are now considerably below historic levels and for a large proportion of the population well below minimum quantities required," the report said.

Five days of rains from July 24 to 28 of between three and five times normal levels flooded parts of the south and southwest, an area the report said produced roughly 60 percent of North Korea's food grain.
It said rice, North Korea's main crop, and maize were at a critical stage of growth when the rains struck.
"Total loss in cereals, due to the floods, is tentatively projected at around 373,000 tonnes including rice in milled equivalent," the report said.
U.N. agencies have put cereal losses from last year's floods at 900,000 tonnes.
"The floods as such were not as severe as in 1995 but the food supply situation will be aggravated," Abdur Rashid, who is in charge of FAO's global information and early warning system, told Reuters.

"In May, we highlighted our estimate that the country would carry over a structural food deficit of more than two million tonnes even under the government's most optimistic scenario. That is not optimistic any more," Rashid said.
He said FAO and WFP would make a further visit to North Korea in October, the harvest period, for a more precise assessment of expected losses.

North Korea, still technically at war with South Korea since a 1950-53 conflict that ended only in a truce, dropped some of its earlier opposition to foreign aid last year to confront the crisis unleashed by the 1995 flooding.

The FAO-WFP report said grain use for livestock had been cut dramatically as the authorities battled shortages and that the government had authorised individual areas to barter products for food directly with neighbouring countries, especially China.
The main commodities bartered included cement, steel and gold. Emergency food aid has also been shipped to the country by U.N. agencies and non-governmental organisations.

The report said FAO and WFP had estimated that pledges and deliveries of food for 1995/96 as a result of barter trade and emergency aid amounted to only 848,300 tonnes of North Korea's import requirement of 1.471 million tonnes.

"This...leaves an overall deficit of some 622,700 tonnes with which the government still needs assistance in the form of programme food aid or concessional commercial imports in order to enable it to maintain minumum ration levels," it said.
